title: Trump AI Task Force Charter Says Labs Are Responsible for Model Risks
summary:
The charter for President Donald Trump's Super Intelligence Force says AI labs are “ultimately responsible” for the risks their models amplify and directs the task force to examine how companies report breaches, hacks and jailbreaks to the government.

The group will examine AI threats to the US water supply and biosecurity, as well as risks to financial services, energy infrastructure, transportation, agriculture and emergency services. It has 120 days to report on AI's risks, opportunities and the federal government's responsibilities, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Trump announced the task force on Oct. 4, naming intelligence chief Jay Clayton, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael and federal personnel director Scott Kupor as its leaders. The industry was not widely briefed before the announcement, Politico reported. Vice President JD Vance and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles will be closely involved, with Condoleezza Rice and David Sacks advising the group.

🇺🇸 The White House launched a Super Intelligence Force with 120 days to map AI's dangers as the industry keeps policing itself

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will chair it, with JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, Scott Bessent and Susie Wiles at the table and Condoleezza Rice advising on security, and its charter calls for plans to handle AI-driven threats without overregulating. 

Clayton framed it as a race:

"The risk of not being first is high."

Putting the nation's top spy in charge treats AI like a security threat, which is the right instinct, but the companies still grade their own homework, so this panel only matters if its report ends with rules that can actually be enforced and followed.

Source: Wall Street Journal / Writer: Daniel

selectedTweets.text:
Anton Leicht says Jay Clayton becoming AI czar of America's new Super Intelligence Force shows Washington now treats AI as a national-security issue:

"It is crazy that within a year we've gone from the AI czar as a venture capitalist, an investor, to the AI czar as the spy chief of the US government. That's a very different vibe."

"How much more of this will be classified. How much more of this will be behind closed doors and only very limited communication between the labs and the US government, but not that much public oversight."

"It would be really good if there were very pronounced checks and balances around what happens on AI policy within the executive. Congress should do something. Third parties should do something."

"The trade-offs that are made there aren't usually as pro-market and pro-diffusion as Silicon Valley might be used to from David Sacks' tenure."
@anton_d_leicht

selectedTweets.text:
President Trump is expected to name his intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, as the White House's new AI czar.

Clayton already oversees 18 intelligence agencies and is expected to keep that post, folding AI policy into the spy portfolio. 

The choice breaks with David Sacks, the venture capitalist who held the post until March and wanted AI left largely unregulated so America could outrun China.

Clayton treats AI as a security problem instead, calling superintelligence "a national security issue" and promising a "whole-of-government approach" to regulating it.

He has still argued against pausing AI, so expect tighter oversight of threats such as AI-enabled hacking without a brake on development.
